title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
subject: Pathology
summary: A sudden, severe bleed into the subarachnoid space, often from a ruptured berry aneurysm. Rapid recognition and treatment are vital to prevent death or severe disability.

sections.p: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the CSF‑filled space surrounding the brain. It is a neurosurgical emergency, presenting most often with a thunderclap headache.

t.b: Detects acute blood in sulci; positive within 6 h of onset
Shows xanthochromia or red cells > 100/µL; confirms SAH when CT is negative
Identifies source (berry aneurysm, AVM, trauma) and guides surgical planning

sections.p: The Hunt‑Hess scale grades clinical severity from I (mild) to V (deep coma). Early grading predicts mortality and guides urgency of intervention.
b: I – mild headache, no neurological deficit
II – moderate headache, mild focal signs

t.b: Higher score correlates with higher mortality and need for early surgery

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the leading causes differ from high‑income countries. Berry aneurysm remains common, but infections and trauma are frequent contributors.
b: Berry aneurysm (Circle of Willis) – 70–80% of spontaneous SAH
Infective causes (tuberculous meningitis, HIV‑associated CNS infections) – 5–10%
Sickle cell disease, malaria, schistosomiasis – rare but possible

t.b: Screen for HIV in patients with unexplained SAH, as HIV can predispose to aneurysm formation
Rule out pulmonary TB that may cause CNS infection

sections.p: The classic thunderclap headache is often accompanied by neck stiffness, photophobia, and sometimes focal neurological signs if a specific vascular territory is involved.
b: Sudden onset, maximum intensity within seconds
Focal deficits (e.g., hemiparesis) if a specific artery is affected

t.b: Assesses level of consciousness; lower scores indicate higher risk of deterioration

sections.p: Rapid imaging is essential. When CT is unavailable, a lumbar puncture can confirm SAH. Angiography identifies the source for definitive treatment.

t.b: Positive if blood seen; negative if no blood but high suspicion
Positive if xanthochromia or >100 red cells/µL
Shows aneurysm, AVM, or traumatic vessel injury

sections.p: Early complications include re‑bleeding, vasospasm, hydrocephalus, and seizures. Red flags for urgent care are worsening headache, new focal deficits, or loss of consciousness.
b: Re‑bleeding – most common cause of death within first 24 h
Vasospasm – peak 4–14 days post‑bleed, causes delayed cerebral ischemia
Hydrocephalus – CSF flow obstruction, needs shunting

t.b: Detects increased flow velocity indicating vasospasm
Shows CSF flow obstruction in hydrocephalus

sections.p: Initial management focuses on securing the airway, preventing re‑bleeding, and controlling blood pressure. Definitive treatment is surgical clipping or endovascular coiling of the aneurysm.

t.b: Calcium channel blocker to reduce risk of vasospasm; given orally or IV
Used only before definitive treatment to reduce re‑bleeding risk

sections.p: Patients require long‑term monitoring for vasospasm, hydrocephalus, and recurrence. Prevention focuses on controlling hypertension and avoiding smoking.
b: Lifestyle modification – stop smoking, control BP

sections.p: Conditions that mimic SAH include migraine, tension headache, and meningitis.
b: Migraine – gradual onset, unilateral, photophobia; no neck stiffness

sections.p: Early CT may be negative if the bleed is small or if the scan is delayed. Lumbar puncture can be falsely normal if performed too early.
b: CT sensitivity >95% within 6 h; drops to 50% after 24 h

t.b: Perform after 6 h if CT negative to avoid false negatives

faq.q: What is the most common source of spontaneous SAH?
faq.a: Berry aneurysm in the Circle of Willis

faq.q: Why is nimodipine used after SAH?
faq.a: It reduces the risk of delayed cerebral vasospasm

faq.q: Can a normal CT rule out SAH?
faq.a: No, a normal CT within 6 h is highly sensitive, but a negative CT after 6 h requires lumbar puncture

exam: A 35‑year‑old presents with a thunderclap headache and neck stiffness. CT is negative. What is the next step? — Perform lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia or >100 red cells/µL; this confirms SAH when CT is negative.

A patient with SAH develops sudden right‑sided weakness 5 days after admission. What complication is most likely? — Delayed cerebral vasospasm; investigate with transcranial Doppler and treat with nimodipine.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in SAH? — They increase bleeding risk and can worsen re‑bleeding.
A patient with known HIV presents with sudden severe headache. What infection should be considered? — Tuberculous meningitis can mimic SAH; CSF analysis and PCR are needed.
What is the first definitive treatment for a ruptured berry aneurysm? — Surgical clipping or endovascular coiling; choice depends on aneurysm location and resources.
A patient with SAH has a GCS of 8. What is the priority? — Secure the airway with intubation to prevent hypoxia and further brain injury.
